newsitem.title: USA: Miami says budget shortfall is city's worst crisis.
newsitem.headline: Miami says budget shortfall is city's worst crisis.

text.p: Miami city officials gave a dire preview Thursday of budget shortfall figures that were expected to be released later in the day.
"The City of Miami is going through its worst financial crisis in its 100-year history," Mayor Joe Corollo said at a city commission meeting.
The mayor said all city employees would be asked to "suck it in and give of themselves to the city," hinting that widespread salary cuts were pending.
"We're going to be asking everyone to bite the bullet," Commissioner Richard Dunn said. "We need cash flow and we need it now."
"We are going to have to make some very hard decisions," said Commissioner Tomas Regalado.
The remarks were made during a city commission meeting, that was to reconvene to deal with the budget Thursday night.

Acting City Manager Merrett Stierheim has said the city expects a budget shortfall for fiscal 1997, which begins Oct 1. He has not disclosed the size of the gap, and skipped the commission's morning session in order to meet with city department heads and union officials.
Carollo said previously the shortfall was about $25 million, or 10 percent of the $250 million operating budget, but declined to reconfirm that estimate Thursday.
Stierheim was to present the final numbers along with proposed remedies Thursday night.

Carollo, Dunn and Regalado made their comments during negotiations with the Parrot Jungle attraction, which sought a 60-year lease on Watson Island, a man-made island in Biscayne Bay owned by the city.
The lease was unanimously approved after Parrot Jungle's owners agreed to increase their payments during the early years of the lease.

The agreement calls for them to pay $200,000 to $400,000 during the first four years of the lease, with payments rising to five percent of gross revenues or at least $400,000 yearly after that. The attraction features botanical gardens and exotic birds and is currently located in southern Dade County.

The budget shortfall was discovered after the resignation of City Manager Cesar Odio, who was charged by federal prosecutors earlier this month with conspiring to solicit bribes in relation to city contracats.
City Commissioner Miller Dawkins was also charged in the bribery case, and prosecutors said former City Finance Director Manohar Surana had agreed to plead guilty on related charges.

Surana resigned in August, shortly before federal prosecutors revealed he had worn a hidden wire to record conversations implicating Odio, Dawkins and a well-known lobbyist. Dunn was chosen to replace Dawkins and Stierheim will replace Odio until a new city manager is hired.
